title: Accuracy
description: Clients don't grade your grammar — but they feel it. Dropped articles and scrambled tenses make you sound unsure, and unsure freelancers don't get hired. The good news: y

steps.body: Clients don't grade your grammar — but they *feel* it. Dropped articles and scrambled tenses make you sound unsure, and unsure freelancers don't get hired. The good news: your errors aren't random. Urdu has no articles, uses postpositions instead of prepositions, and builds time differently — so your mistakes follow predictable patterns. Fix the pattern once, and dozens of individual errors disappear. This module targets your six interference points in order of client impact.

steps.heading: How to use this module
steps.body:
One topic per ~4 days. Read the contrastive explanation (Urdu ↔ English — this is deliberate: seeing the difference kills the error at its root), do the examples aloud, then hit the drills at the end. Log every error you make into your error log.

---

steps.heading: The Urdu problem
steps.body: Urdu has no articles at all. You can't translate what doesn't exist — so learners either drop them (*"make Etsy account"*) or panic-insert them (*"make a n Etsy account"* — your actual message). Pakistani research found 83% of article errors are with a/an, and over half are simple omission.

steps.heading: The system (learn this, not a list of rules)
steps.body:
Think of articles as answering the listener's question: *"Which one?"*

- **First mention, one of many → a/an:** *"I built **a** dashboard."* (One dashboard among many possible. Listener thinks: okay, a dashboard.)
- **Already known / specific → the:** *"**The** dashboard is ready."* (Now we both know which one.)
- **Plural or uncountable, general → nothing:** *"I build dashboards." / "I need information."*

steps.heading: Still articles — new reps
steps.body: Same system as Part 1: **a/an** = first mention, **the** = the listener knows which one. These reps mix every article rule — say each fixed sentence out loud.

steps.heading: a vs an — the only rule
steps.body: use **an** before vowel *sounds* (an apple, an hour, an Etsy account — "Etsy" starts with an E sound), **a** before consonant sounds (a university — "university" starts with a Y sound!).

steps.heading: The freelancer's shortcut
steps.body: memorize articles *inside chunks*, not as rules. Your mouth learns "make **an** appointment", "**a** fixed quote", "**the** client", "**the** deadline" as whole pieces. In a live call you won't have time to compute rules — chunks fire instantly.

steps.heading: Contrastive corner (Urdu ↔ English)
steps.body:
Urdu (no article needed) · English (article required)
Main ne dashboard banaya. · I built a dashboard. (first mention)
Wo dashboard tayyar hai. · The dashboard is ready. (we know which)
Mujhe information chahiye. · I need some information. (uncountable — never "an information")
Ek Etsy account banao. · Make an Etsy account. ("ek" ≈ "a/an" only for first mention!)
steps.tip: Warning: Don't map Urdu "ek" → "a" everywhere. "Ek" works for first mention (ek client → a client), but the has no Urdu equivalent — learn it as "the one we both know."

steps.heading: The Urdu problem
steps.body:
Urdu countability doesn't match English. So *"advices," "informations," "homeworks"* feel natural — but they're wrong, and they jump out in client writing.

**The closed list** (memorize these 12 — they cover nearly all client situations): **advice, information, homework, work, news, furniture, luggage, equipment, money, knowledge, progress, feedback.** All uncountable: no -s, no "a/an". Workarounds: *a piece of **advice***, *some **information***, *two items of **feedback***.

steps.heading: Your error, fixed
steps.body: *"Give me some advices"* → *"Give me some **advice**."*

steps.heading: SRS card format for these
steps.body:
never "advice = ?". Always the chunk: front → *"Give me some ___ (advice)"*, back → *"Give me some **advice**."* The quantifier rides along with the word.

---

steps.heading: The Urdu problem
steps.body: Urdu is SOV — verb goes last. *"Yeh kitaab main parh raha hoon"* = literally "this book I reading am." Your brain composes in Urdu, then translates — and the verb lands in the wrong place: *"This book I'm reading"* instead of *"I'm reading this book."* Research with Urdu-L1 students found this transfer "inevitable" and even subconscious at advanced levels.

steps.heading: The one rule
steps.body:
**In English, the verb comes second. In Urdu, the verb comes last.** That's it. One systematic difference, drilled until it's a motor habit.

Urdu order (SOV) · English order (SVO)
Main kal client se mila. (I yesterday client met) · I met the client yesterday.
Us ne file bheji hai. (He file sent has) · He has sent the file.
Tum kya kar rahe ho? (You what doing are?) · What are you doing?

steps.heading: The time-word trap
steps.body: Urdu puts time words early (*"kal main..."*). English prefers them at the end or start — but the verb still stays second: *"**Yesterday** I **met** the client"* or *"I **met** the client **yesterday**."* Never *"I yesterday met the client."*

steps.prompt:
**Back-translation relay**

Take these Urdu sentences, translate to English (SVO! verb second!), then translate your English BACK to Urdu. Where the round trip breaks, your word order broke:
1. Main ne kal client ko email bheji.
2. Wo is project par do hafte se kaam kar raha hai.
3. Tum ne file kab bheji thi?
Model: 1. I sent the client an email yesterday. 2. He has been working on this project for two weeks. 3. When did you send the file?

steps.heading: The Urdu problem
steps.body: Urdu uses postpositions (*mein, se, ko, par*) that come AFTER the word, and one Urdu word covers many English ones. Urdu *se* alone can mean *of, with,* or *from*. So your brain picks one English preposition per Urdu word — and it's wrong 72% of the time (that's the documented substitution rate).

steps.heading: The rule that replaces translation
steps.body:
**Never translate prepositions. Learn them as chunks.**

These 20 chunks cover 90% of client-call prepositions. Learn each as one unbreakable piece:

- interested **in**, good **at**, responsible **for**, depend **on**, wait **for**, married **to**, agree **with** (a person) / agree **to** (a proposal) / agree **on** (a price), angry **with**, afraid **of**, different **from**, discuss **∅** (no preposition! "discuss the project", never "discuss about"), work **on** (a project), work **for** (a client), work **with** (a team), apply **for** (a job), ask **for** (a raise), belong **to**, consist **of**, deal **with**, follow up **on**, get back **to** you, look forward **to** meeting you.

steps.heading: Your error, fixed
steps.body: *"She is married with Ali"* → *"She is married **to** Ali."* (Married takes **to**. Always. It's a chunk.)

steps.heading: The since/for trap (time prepositions)
steps.body: **since** = starting point (*since 2021, since Monday*). **for** = duration (*for 3 years, for six months*). Urdu doesn't split these — English does. Client sentence: *"I have been learning Python **since** 2024"* vs *"I have been learning Python **for** two years."*

steps.heading: The Urdu problem
steps.body:
Urdu marks time with helpers (*hai, tha, hoga*) and verb shapes, not with English's tense+aspect machinery. Result: *"I was working pastly in 2021 2024"* (wrong tense + invented adverb) and *"I have saw"* (right helper, wrong participle). Pakistani learners' most frequent tense error is actually the simple present (*"he work"* — dropping the -s), with present perfect confusion close behind.

**Learn tenses as timelines, not tables.** For freelancing, you need exactly four uses of the present perfect (**have/has + past participle**):

1. **Life experience (your portfolio):** *"I **have built** three dashboards."* (At some point in your life, unspecified when. This is how you talk about skills without faking timelines.)
2. **Recent result:** *"I **have just finished** the data cleaning."* (Done very recently — the result matters now.)
3. **Duration continuing now:** *"I **have worked** with Python **for** two years."* (Started in the past, still true.)
4. **Unfinished time:** *"I **have sent** two proposals this week."* (This week isn't over.)

steps.heading: The contrast that matters
steps.body: *"I **worked** on this project in 2023"* (finished, closed chapter — simple past) vs *"I **have worked** on this project"* (experience I carry with me — present perfect). On a client call, use present perfect for your skills and simple past for finished stories.

steps.heading: Your error, fixed
steps.body:
*"I was working pastly in 2021 2024"* → *"I **worked** as a sales supervisor **from** 2021 **to** 2024."* (Finished period → simple past. "Pastly" isn't a word — and "from X to Y" is the chunk for ranges.)

**Participle watch-list** (the irregulars Pakistani learners actually mix up): see→**seen**, do→**done**, go→**gone**, write→**written**, build→**built**, send→**sent**, speak→**spoken**, take→**taken**. (*"I have saw"* → *"I have **seen**."*)

steps.prompt:
**Timeline mapping**

Draw a line. Mark 2021, 2024, and NOW. Place these events, then write each as a sentence choosing simple past or present perfect:
1. Your sales supervisor job (2021–2024, finished)
2. Starting BS Data Science (2024, still studying)
3. A Python project you finished last month
4. A skill you have been building since January
Then explain to your AI tutor WHY you chose each tense. The explaining is the learning.

steps.heading: The problem
steps.body: English adds **-s** for he/she/it in the present: *he works, she goes.* It's tiny, it's redundant (the "he" already tells you who's acting), so your brain drops it: *"he work."* You usually KNOW this rule — it's a monitoring problem, not a knowledge problem.

steps.heading: The fix is a habit, not a lesson
steps.body: after writing anything for a client, circle every verb with a he/she/it subject and check the -s. In speech, shadowing native audio builds the *expectation* of hearing that -s, which slowly fixes production.

steps.heading: Priority note
steps.body: this error is high-visibility in *writing* (proposals, emails — clients read those slowly) and low-visibility in *speech* (calls move fast). Fix it in writing first.

steps.heading: The doesn't/don't pair
steps.body: *he/she/it* → **doesn't** (*"He **doesn't** have time"* — your placement item 8). Everything else → **don't**. One of the most common slips in South Asian English; clients notice it instantly.

steps.heading: Can-do statements
steps.body:
- [ ] I can explain when to use a/an/the/the-nothing using the "which one?" test
- [ ] I know 20+ preposition chunks by heart and never translate prepositions from Urdu
- [ ] I can choose simple past vs present perfect by asking "finished chapter or living experience?"
- [ ] My verbs sit in second position automatically, even in long sentences
- [ ] I check he/she/it verbs for -s before sending any client writing

steps.heading: Mini-test
steps.body: Write 6 client sentences, each demonstrating one lesson: (1) an article rule, (2) a preposition chunk, (3) present perfect for experience, (4) SVO order with a time word, (5) a he/she/it verb, (6) an uncountable noun. Send them to your AI tutor for the strict correction pass.

steps.heading: Re-entry note
steps.body:
Back after a break? Don't reread all six lessons. Open your error log, find your most frequent error type, and redo just that lesson's drill. Accuracy is maintained by sprints, not marathons.

🎯 **Badge earned: Article Ace** — your sentences are now client-safe on paper. Next: making them client-clear out loud.
